subject: Multiple group longitudinal 2PL IRT model using SEM framework

messages.author: ed404d405a3e6877
messages.subject: Multiple group longitudinal 2PL IRT model using SEM framework
parts:
Hi All,
 
I have been fitting 2-parameter logistic multi-group longitudinal IRT models using a Bayesian approach. I was wondering whether the SEM approach using the WLSMV  in lavaan would be a faster alternative. So far I have implemented the population-averaged longitudinal models, where abilities are represented by a separate latent variable at each time point with a covariance structure for the multple latent variables.
I have also implemented a linear random coefficients  mixed model, where the latent ability is a linear function of time (could also use quadratic I suppose). - Both using the Bayesian approach.
 
I have seen the SEM approach for the linear random coefficients mixed model approach, but I have not seen the SEM approach for the populaiton-averaged model - is it possible to represent such a model in the SEM framework?
 
I have also looked at the Latent Growh Model code in the Mplus manual, but have not been able to implement something similar in lavaan.
I would appreciate if the lavaan community could point me to any lavaan code/source that implements multiple group longitudinal IRT models.
Many thanks in advance!

messages.author: 7406e44d979f1add
messages.subject: Re: Multiple group longitudinal 2PL IRT model using SEM framework
parts:
Hi Yves, 

The usual modeling framework that comes to mind in distinguishing population averaged from individual level is generalized estimating equations: basically a marginal modeling approach using robust (sandwich based) Huber White variance estimators. The original article from Liang and Zeger 1973 describes estimating equations, sandwich errors, and their asymptotic properties. One of their advantages is that they provide consistent error estimation regardless of correct model specification, or any kind of parametric model for the errors.

I'm a little hesitant to suggest sandwich errors would be appropriate in an SEM framework. One of the key assumptions to SEM, in my mind, is the nature of the underlying normal distribution of endogenous or exogenous variables so that 0 covariance implies conditional independence.
